name: MapReduce and Shuffles
intent: Process data too big for one machine by mapping it in parallel, regrouping it by key across the network (the shuffle), and reducing each group.
scenario: A job counts page views per URL over 2,000 log lines. Two mappers each read 1,000 lines and emit (url, 1) records. A shuffle sends every record for the same URL to the same one of two reducers, which sum them. One URL, /home, is 60% of all traffic.
problem: Aggregating or joining by key needs every record for a key in one place, but the data is spread over hundreds of machines. Moving it naively floods the network, and a few popular keys can leave one machine doing most of the work while the rest sit idle.

howItWorks.title: Map: run user code next to the data
howItWorks.text: The input is cut into splits (often one per 128 MB to 256 MB storage block). A mapper task reads one split, applies your function and emits (key, value) records. Map tasks are independent, so thousands can run in parallel and a failed one is simply re-run.

howItWorks.title: Combine and spill: shrink data before it leaves
howItWorks.text: Mapper output is buffered in memory, partitioned by hash(key) mod number-of-reducers, sorted and spilled to local disk (not to a replicated filesystem). An optional combiner pre-aggregates inside the mapper, which is valid only when the operation is associative and commutative, like sum, count or max, and can shrink shuffle volume by 10x to 1000x on repetitive keys.

howItWorks.title: Shuffle: an all-to-all network copy
howItWorks.text: Each reducer pulls its partition from every mapper, so M mappers and R reducers mean up to M x R transfers. This is usually the slowest and most failure-prone stage: it needs disk and network on every node, and lost map output means re-running those mappers.

howItWorks.title: Merge: sort so equal keys are adjacent
howItWorks.text: A reducer merge-sorts the sorted runs it fetched, so all values for one key are contiguous and it can stream through them with little memory. Spark and Hive can instead use hash aggregation, but every approach needs all records of a key on one task.

howItWorks.title: Reduce: one call per key, then write
howItWorks.text: The reduce function sees (key, all values) and emits results to the output files, one per reducer. The job finishes only when the slowest reducer does, so the work per reducer matters more than the average.

howItWorks.title: Handle skew and pick the partition count
howItWorks.text: Hash partitioning balances keys, not records. A hot key goes to one reducer whatever the reducer count. Fixes include combiners, salting the hot key and merging in a second stage, a broadcast join for a small table, or letting the engine split skewed partitions at run time (Spark adaptive query execution). A common target is 100 MB to 1 GB per partition: thousands of tiny partitions drown in scheduling overhead, a few huge ones spill and cannot parallelise.

pros: Simple model: you write two functions, the framework handles distribution, retries and sorting
Scales by adding machines and works on data far larger than any machine's memory
Failed tasks are re-run, because map and reduce are deterministic and map output is on local disk
The same shuffle idea powers Spark, Hive, Flink batch, BigQuery and Snowflake joins and group-bys
cons: The shuffle is expensive: it writes to disk, crosses the network and sorts, so it often dominates job time
Hot keys make one reducer a straggler, and adding reducers does not fix it
Latency is minutes to hours: it is a batch model, not for interactive or per-event answers
Chains of jobs write intermediate data to disk between stages, which is slow for iterative algorithms
whenToUse: Large offline aggregations, joins and rebuilds over terabytes of data where minutes of latency are fine
Reprocessing history after a logic fix, where you can re-run the job from raw files
Whenever you choose a partition key or a join strategy in Spark or SQL, because the shuffle is what you are paying for
whenNotToUse: Data that fits on one machine: a single process or a database query is faster and far simpler than a cluster
Low-latency or per-event results, where a stream processor or an indexed store fits better
Iterative or interactive workloads written as raw MapReduce, where in-memory engines avoid the disk round trip between stages
pitfalls: Using a combiner for a non-associative operation such as average or median: combine sums and counts and divide at the end instead
Partitioning on a low-cardinality or skewed column (country, a null key), so most records land on a handful of reducers
Leaving the default shuffle partition count (200 in Spark SQL) regardless of data size, producing tiny or enormous tasks
Joining two large datasets on a key with many nulls: all null keys hash to the same reducer
Reading the average task time instead of the maximum: one straggler hides behind a healthy mean
Assuming reducers are idempotent when they write to an external system, so a retried task double-counts

roles.label: Input splits
roles.description: The data cut into blocks, each read by one map task.

roles.label: Mapper
roles.description: Runs the map function and combiner, then writes partitioned, sorted output to local disk.

roles.label: Reducer
roles.description: Pulls its partition from every mapper, merges it and runs the reduce function per key.
